## Introduction & background

RF engineering runs on S-parameters (Scattering parameters). Instead of measuring absolute voltages and currents (which is incredibly difficult at microwaves), engineers measure power ratios. $S_{11}$ represents "Return Loss"—the ratio of power reflected *back* out of a port compared to the power injected into it. A perfectly matched antenna absorbs all energy, meaning zero is reflected, giving an $S_{11}$ approaching $-\infty$ dB. A terrible antenna reflects almost everything, giving an $S_{11}$ near 0 dB. Converting $S_{11}$ into a linear reflection coefficient ($\Gamma$), percentage of power reflected, and Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) is a reflex every hardware engineer must build.

## Core equations

Return Loss (dB):
$$S_{11(dB)} = 20 \log_{10}(|\Gamma|)$$

VSWR:
$$VSWR = \frac{1 + |\Gamma|}{1 - |\Gamma|}$$

## What you're building

1. A calculated reference table translating four common $S_{11}$ benchmarks (-3, -6, -10, and -20 dB) into their exact $|\Gamma|$, Power Reflected %, and VSWR equivalents.
2. A Python script utilizing the `scikit-rf` library to mathematically model AC impedance over frequency.
3. Plotted $S_{11}$ vs. frequency graphs (1 MHz–1 GHz) for both a pure 100 Ω resistive load and a 10 pF capacitive load.

## Activity

Build this table by hand: S11 = −3 / −6 / −10 / −20 dB → |Γ| → % power reflected → VSWR. Then `pip install scikit-rf` and plot S11 vs frequency (1 MHz–1 GHz) for (a) a series 100 Ω load and (b) 10 pF to ground.
